en: Maṅgala S,1: He who, having abandoned his primordial form, manifests in manifold ways for the sake of bestowing grace upon the world; [having abandoned, he is the Lord].

Maṅgala S,1: His mass of afflictions is utterly destroyed, yet he is like poison though not a venomous serpent, possessing many faces and great enjoyment; [his afflictions destroyed, not a venomous serpent, great enjoyment].

May that Lord of Serpents, the source of all knowledge, whose body is white and stainless, who is ever delighted by his serpent-retinue, and who is united with yoga through yoga— may he protect you. Now, the instruction on yoga (atha yogānuśāsanam).
YBh 1.1(1): Now, the word "atha" (now) serves as an introductory marker (*adhikāra*). YBh 1.1(2): Yoga is *samādhi* (concentration).
YBh 1.1(2): And that is a quality (*dharma*) of the mind (*citta*) belonging to all stages (*sārva-bhauma*).
[It] loosens the afflictions and the bonds of karma; [it is] followed by the cessation of the sense of "I-am-ness. Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind.
YBh 1.2(4): For the mind (citta) consists of the three *guṇas*, because its nature is characterized by manifestation (*prakhyā*), activity (*pravṛtti*), and stability (*sthiti*).

YBh 1.2(5): That very same [mind], when permeated by *tamas* (*anuviddha*), becomes associated with demerit (*adharma*), ignorance (*ajñāna*), lack of dispassion (*avairāgya*), and lack of mastery (*anaiśvarya*).
[The roots *anu-vyadh* and *pra-dyut* are used here.]

YBh 1.2(5): That very [citta], when freed from the stain of even a trace of *rajas* and established in its own nature, becomes nothing but the discriminative discernment (*anyatākhyāti*) between *sattva* and the Puruṣa; it approaches the *dharmamegha* meditation. [It is established. YBh 1.2(5–6):
Meditators call that the supreme *prasaṃkhyāna*. YBh 1.2(6):

The power of consciousness (*citiśakti*) is unchanging, non-transferring, has objects presented to it, is pure, infinite, and consists of the quality of *sattva*. Discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), however, is the opposite of this. [Change (*pariṇāma*)]
...transforming, [changing].

YBh 1.2 (6): Therefore, the mind, becoming detached from that [state], suppresses even that cognitive manifestation (*khyāti*). [from *vi-raj* and *ni-rudh*] YBh 1.2 (6): It becomes a state consisting solely of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
That is seedless (nirbīja) samādhi.
Because nothing is cognized therein, it is called "non-cognitive" (asamprajñāta). That yoga, which is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind, is of two kinds.
How then [is it]?
Because its object has been presented,
there is conformity with the mental modification in other cases.
And likewise, the Sūtra says: “Vision is one alone; manifestation itself is vision.
(YS 1.4) The mind, like a magnet, assists by its mere proximity and becomes the object of perception for its master, the Puruṣa.
(YBh 1.4) The fluctuations are of five kinds, both afflicted and unafflicted. [They are to be restrained. (YS 1.5)
Even those [mental modifications] that fall within a stream of afflicted ones may be unafflicted;
likewise, such formative impressions (saṃskāras) are produced by the mental modifications themselves.
In this way, the wheel of mental modifications and their formative impressions revolves incessantly.
YBh 1.5(10): That mind, having thus fulfilled its purpose, remains in a state resembling the Self, or it undergoes dissolution.

[from ava-so and vyava-sthā] YS 1.7(10): Direct perception, inference, and verbal testimony are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). YBh 1.7(11): The result is the awareness of the mental modifications by the Puruṣa, which is not distinct from them. [from vi-śiṣ]

YBh 1.7 (11): We shall establish later that the person (*puruṣa*) is the experiencer (*pratisaṃvedin*). [The roots *prati-sam-vid* and *upa-pad*... And the Vindhya mountain is non-attainment (*aprāpti*), which is non-motion (*agati*).
YBh 1.8 (13): Why is that not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
Since the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has as its object the real nature of things,
ignorance (*avidyā*) arises; and ignorance, egoism (*asmitā*), attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and the will to cling (*abhiniveśa*) are the afflictions (*kleśa*).
YBh 1.8 (13): These very [afflictions] are designated by their own names as *tamas*, *moha*, *mahāmoha*, *tāmisra*, and *andhatāmisra*.
YS 1.9 (13): Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is that which follows upon the cognition of a word and is devoid of a real object.
YBh 1.9 (13): It does not fall within the scope of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
YBh 1.9 (13): [The definition of knowledge] does not ascend to the state of error.
YBh 1.9 (14): For example—consciousness is the essential nature of the *puruṣa*.
YBh 1.9 (14): When consciousness itself is the *puruṣa*, then what is designated here by what?
Just as in the case of "Caitra’s cow," [or] "the arrow stands, will stand, has stood"—
[this is the negation of change]— so too is the person (puruṣa) characterized by the property of non-arising.
Only the mere absence of that which has the nature of arising is understood, not a quality (dharma) inherent in the Puruṣa. [The roots *ava-gam* and *anvaya* are used here.
YS 1.10: Sleep is a mental modification (*vṛtti*) whose object is the notion of non-existence.
YBh 1.10: How so? "I slept happily. [The root *svap* is used here.]

YBh 1.10(15): "My mind is serene; it makes my wisdom confident. YBh 1.10(15): "I slept poorly; my mind is sluggish and wandering, lacking stability. YBh 1.10(15): "I slept in a state of deep delusion. [√svap]
"My limbs are heavy;
my mind is exhausted;
it remains as if sluggish and robbed of its clarity."
YS 1.11: Memory is the non-loss of an experienced object. YBh 1.11:
Does the mind remember the cognition (*pratyaya*), or rather the object? YBh 1.11:
That latent impression (*saṃskāra*), when manifested by its own manifestor, produces a memory that consists of both the grasped and the grasping, and which bears the very form of that [object].

In this regard, cognition (*buddhi*) is preceded by the form of the apprehension; memory (*smṛti*) is preceded by the form of the object to be apprehended. And that [memory] is of two kinds: that in which the object to be remembered has been cultivated (*bhāvitasmartavyā*), and that in which the object to be remembered has not been cultivated (*abhāvitasmartavyā*).
Attachment is that which lies latent in pleasure;
aversion is that which lies latent in pain;
and delusion, moreover, is ignorance.
YS 1.12: Their cessation is achieved through practice and dispassion.
YBh 1.12: The river of the mind flows in two directions; it flows toward both what is auspicious and what is evil.
That which tends toward isolation (*kaivalya*) and inclines toward the object of discriminative discernment is the one that flows toward what is auspicious.
YBh 1.12: [The mind] is inclined toward the world of transmigration, flows downward toward objects of non-discrimination, and carries away evil.
YBh 1.13: Stability is the tranquil flow of the mind when it is free from fluctuations.
YS 1.15: Dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the consciousness of mastery in one who is free from thirst for objects perceived through experience or heard through scripture.
That [discriminative discernment] is of two kinds of detachment (*vairāgya*).
Of these, that which is the higher consists solely of the clarity of knowledge (*jñānaprasāda*);
the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be destroyed have been destroyed.
Because of its non-interruption, one dies after being born, and is born again after dying.
(YBh 1.16) Dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the supreme limit of knowledge.
For it is this [dispassion] alone that has liberation (*kaivalya*) as its necessary consequence.
YS 1.17: Samprajñāta [samādhi] occurs through the accompaniment of the forms of vitarka (gross reflection), vicāra (subtle reflection), ānanda (bliss), and asmitā (I-am-ness).
YBh 1.17: Asmitā is the consciousness that has become one with the Self.
YBh 1.17: Among these, the first samādhi, which is accompanied by all four, is savitarka. [The root *anu-gam* means "to accompany" or "to follow along with."]
YBh 1.17 (21): The fourth [type of samādhi] is deficient in those [other factors] and consists of mere *asmitā* (I-am-ness).
All these types of samādhi have an object of focus (*sālambana*).
YBh 1.18 (21): Now, what is the means for *asamprajñāta* samādhi, and what is its essential nature?
The means for that [cessation] is supreme detachment (*vairāgya*).
And that [detachment] is devoid of objects.
For, preceded by the practice of that [detachment], the mind becomes objectless, as if it has reached non-existence; this is seedless (*nirbīja*) samādhi, which is *asamprajñāta*.
For the bodiless gods (*videha*), the cause is existence (*bhava-pratyaya*) until the mind returns again by virtue of its office (*adhikāra*).
For others, [the cause is] preceded by faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
YBh 1.20: Faith is the clarity of the mind.
For it protects the yogi like a virtuous mother.
Indeed, in one who possesses faith and seeks discriminative discernment, vigor arises. [śrad-dhā]
For one in whom vigor has arisen, mindfulness becomes established (*upatiṣṭhate*).
For one whose mind is concentrated (*samāhita*), discernment through wisdom (*prajñāviveka*) returns (*upāvartate*).
By means of this, one knows the object as it truly is (*yathārtham vastu jānāti*).
YBh 1.20: Through the practice of that [samādhi] and through detachment from its respective objects, *asamprajñāta* samādhi arises.
YBh 1.21: Indeed, those nine types of yogins possess mild, medium, or intense means (*upāya*). Thus, there are those with medium means and those with intense means.
In that regard, for those possessing superior means— namely,
those with intense spiritual urgency— the attainment of samādhi and the fruit of samādhi are near at hand.
YS 1.22: There is a distinction even from that, due to being mild, moderate, or intense.
YBh 1.22: There is a distinction even from that.
Due to that distinction, for one whose impulse is mild-intense, [success] is near; for one whose impulse is moderately-intense, it is nearer still.
Therefore, for one who possesses intense urgency (*saṃvega*) and employs superior means (*upāya*), the attainment of samādhi and its fruit are most immediate.
[Up to this point] YBh 1.23(25): Is samādhi attained as something most immediate only through this [intense practice]?
YS 1.23(25): Or rather, through devotion to Īśvara (*īśvara-praṇidhāna*).

YBh 1.23: Through his resolve and through a special devotion, Īśvara is won over; he favors the yogin by mere meditation [upon him]. YBh 1.23: Even from that mere meditation, for the yogin, the attainment of samādhi becomes most immediate, as does the fruit of samādhi.
YS 1.24: Īśvara is a distinct puruṣa, untouched by afflictions (kleśa), actions (karman), their ripening (vipāka), or latent dispositions (āśaya).
Ignorance and the others are the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Wholesome and unwholesome actions are karma.
The fruition of that [karma] is maturation (*vipāka*).
The latent dispositions (*vāsanā*) that conform to those [fluctuations] are the impressions (*āśaya*).

Just as a prior limit of bondage is known for one who has been liberated, it does not exist for the Lord (*īśvara*). Or, just as a future limit of bondage is conceivable for one who is merged in *prakṛti*, it is not so for the Lord.
But He is eternally liberated and eternally the Lord.
(YBh 1.24) That eternal excellence of the Lord, which arises from His assumption of preeminent *sattva*, is it caused or is it causeless?
(YBh 1.24) Scripture is its cause.
YBh 1.24: Furthermore, for what purpose is the scripture?
It has as its purpose those of superior sattva.
From this it follows that the Lord is eternally so and eternally liberated.
And that sovereignty of His is free from both equality and superiority.
For whatever might be superior would itself be that [very sovereignty]. Therefore, He in whom there is the ultimate limit of sovereignty is the Lord (Īśvara).
Furthermore, there is no such thing as equal sovereignty [between two beings].
For it is impossible for two equals to simultaneously attain their desired object,
because the objects [of desire] are mutually exclusive.
Therefore, he whose sovereignty is free from degrees of excellence or deficiency is indeed the Lord (Īśvara). And He is a particular kind of Puruṣa.
Furthermore:
In that regard, the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed.

That which consists in the apprehension of the past, future, and present—whether individually or collectively—and which transcends the senses, whether it be small or great, is the seed of omniscience; as this increases until it reaches its limit, he in whom it is unsurpassed is the omniscient one.
There is a reaching of the ultimate limit for the seed of omniscience because it is subject to degrees of excellence, just like physical dimension.
YBh 1.25(30): That in which there is the ultimate limit of knowledge is the omniscient one.
And he is a particular kind of *puruṣa*.
The specific understanding of his names and other attributes is to be sought from scripture (*āgama*).
YBh 1.26: This is that [Ishvara]. YS 1.27: The syllable Om (praṇava) is its designator.
YBh 1.27: Ishvara is the designated object of the syllable Om.

For the yogi who has understood the relationship between the signified and the signifier, there is the repetition of that [sacred syllable] and the contemplation of its meaning. (YS 1.28) The repetition of the *praṇava* and the contemplation of the Lord (*īśvara*), who is denoted by the *praṇava*. [abhi-dhā]
YBh 1.28: For this yogin who repeats the *praṇava* and meditates upon the meaning of the *praṇava*, the mind becomes one-pointed.
And so it has been said: "From self-study one should practice yoga; from yoga one should practice self-study.
Furthermore, what else happens for him?
YS 1.29: From that, there arises the realization of the inward-turned consciousness and the absence of obstacles.
YBh 1.29: There also occurs for him the perception of his own true nature.
YBh 1.30: Now, what are the obstacles? They are the distractions of the mind.
What, then, are these [obstacles], and how many are they?
Illness, languor, doubt, heedlessness, laziness, lack of dispassion, erroneous perception, failure to attain a stage, and instability—these distractions of the mind are the obstacles.
There are nine obstacles which are distractions of the mind.
These [obstacles] exist together with the fluctuations of the mind. Disease is a disorder of the humors, the elements, or the sense organs. Lethargy is the lack of functional capacity of the mind.

YBh 1.30: Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is a cognition that touches upon two alternatives, such as "it might be thus" or "it might not be thus. YBh 1.30: Negligence (*pramāda*) is the failure to cultivate the means for achieving *samādhi*.
YBh 1.30: Laziness (*ālasya*) is the lack of application due to heaviness of both body and mind.

YBh 1.30 (34): Erroneous perception is knowledge based on misconception. These nine distractions of the mind are called the impurities of yoga, the adversaries of yoga, and the obstacles to yoga. YBh 1.31 (35): Suffering is internal, external [due to other beings], and celestial [due to divine forces].
[Regarding the categories of] *adhibhūta* and *adhidaiva*:
that by which living beings are struck and strive to repel it is suffering (*duḥkha*). Dejection (*daurmanasya*) is the agitation of the mind resulting from the frustration of one's desires.
YBh 1.31 (35): That which causes the limbs to quiver or shake is "limb-trembling" (*aṅgamejayatva*). YBh 1.31 (35): That which expels the internal air from the chest is exhalation (*praśvāsa*).
YBh 1.31 (35): These do not occur for one whose mind is concentrated (*samāhitacitta*).

Now, these distractions are the adversaries of samādhi; they are to be suppressed by those very two: practice (*abhyāsa*) and detachment (*vairāgya*). In this regard, while summarizing the object of practice, he says: "For the purpose of suppressing them, practice on a single principle (*ekatattvābhyāsa*). (YS 1.32)
YBh 1.32: For the purpose of preventing distraction, one should practice the mind by making it rest upon a single principle (*ekatattva*).

For one, however, for whom the mind consists merely of momentary cognitions fixed upon their respective objects, every state of that mind is indeed one-pointed; there is no such thing as a distracted mind at all.
Now, [if it is argued that] this property belongs only to a cognition that is a part of the mental stream, [then...]
Therefore, the mind is one, has many objects, and is stable.
[The state of stability] Even when this [mind] is somehow being concentrated, it brings to mind the analogy of cow-dung and milk-porridge.
[To bring to mind] Therefore, the mind is one, has many objects, and is stable.

YS 1.33: Through the cultivation of friendliness, compassion, joy, and equanimity toward objects that are happy, suffering, virtuous, and non-virtuous, there is clarity of the mind. YBh 1.33: And from that, the mind becomes clear. YBh 1.33: Being clear, it becomes one-pointed and attains a state of stability.

YS 1.34: By means of exhalation (*pracchardana*) and retention (*vidhāraṇa*) of the breath, or by the restraint (*vidhāraṇa*) of the breath itself, one may achieve steadiness of the mind through those two. YS 1.35: Alternatively, an activity of the mind directed toward an object, once arisen, serves as a basis for the steadiness of the mind.
YBh 1.35(39): [The internal sounds] produce cognition of form in the palate, dispel doubt, and serve as gateways to the wisdom of samādhi. [This concludes the section on the bond.]
...[the gate]...

YBh 1.35 (40): By this [same principle], it should be understood that the activity which has arisen with respect to the rays of the moon, the sun, planets, jewels, lamps, and so forth, is indeed possessed of an object (*viṣayavat*). For even though the reality of an object is understood through those respective scriptures, inference, and the instructions of teachers, it remains truly existent because these [means] possess the capacity to represent the object as it actually is.

Therefore, for the sake of corroborating the scriptures, inference, and the instructions of the teacher, some specific object must necessarily be made directly perceptible. It is for this very purpose that this mental purification (*cittaparikarma*) is prescribed. When the notion of mastery (*vaśīkārasaṃjñā*) regarding those objects has arisen amidst fluctuating mental states, one will be capable of making each respective object directly perceptible. [Direct perception]

YS 1.36: Or, it is the luminous [meditative state] which is free from sorrow. YBh 1.36: It follows that "the activity which has arisen is the cause of the mind's stability. For the *sattva* of the intellect (*buddhisattva*) is radiant, like space.

Likewise, when the mind has attained the state of *asmitā* (I-am-ness), it becomes like a great ocean without waves—tranquil, infinite, and consisting of *asmitā* alone. Regarding this, it is said: "Having discerned that self which is subtle as an atom, one recognizes it thus: 'I am'. This twofold [samādhi], free from sorrow, possesses an object.
The activity characterized by the mere sense of "I-am-ness" (asmitāmātrā) is called luminous (jyotiṣmatī),
by which the yogi’s mind attains the state of stability. Or, the mind has as its object one who is free from passion (vītarāga).
YBh 1.37: Or, the yogi’s mind, colored by having the mind of one free from passion as its object, attains a state of stability. [from the root *uparañj*] YS 1.38:
Or, it has the knowledge of dreaming or the knowledge of sleep as its object.
YBh 1.38: Or, the yogi’s mind, taking the knowledge of dreaming as its object or the knowledge of sleep as its object, attains a state of stability by assuming their form.

"Or from meditation on whatever is desired. (YS 1.39) One should meditate on that very thing which is desired. Having attained stability therein, it attains a state of stability elsewhere as well. (YBh 1.39)

YBh 1.40: Through mastery over that [mind], the yogin’s mind becomes perfected; it no longer requires the preparatory refinement produced by practice. YBh 1.41: Now, for the mind that has attained stability, what is the nature of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), and what is its object? To this it is said: YBh 1.41: Colored by the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*), the mind enters into the subtle elements and comes to appear as the very form of those subtle elements.

In the same way, [the mind] becomes colored by a gross object, attains the state of a gross form, and appears as a gross form. Likewise, it becomes colored by the diversity of the universe, attains the state of universal diversity, and appears as the form of the universe. Among these, the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) that is mixed with the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of word, meaning, and knowledge is called "with deliberation" (*savitarka*).

YBh 2.34 (106): "Those whose fruits are infinite suffering and ignorance"—this is the cultivation of the counter-measures.
And so it is: first of all, the one who harms robs the victim of his vitality.
From that, he even deprives [beings] of their life.
From that, due to the projection of his own vigor (*vīrya*), his animate and inanimate implements become devoid of vigor.
Because he causes suffering, he experiences suffering among hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts (*preta*), and so forth.
YBh 2.34 (107): In this same manner, [the consequences] should be applied to falsehood and the other [vices] as well, according to their possibility.
YBh 2.35 (107): For example:
it occurs for all living beings.
YS 2.36: When truth is firmly established, there is the attainment of the fruits of action. [For example,] when one says, "Attain heaven," he attains heaven; his word becomes infallible.
YS 2.37: When non-stealing is firmly established, all jewels present themselves to him.

YBh 2.38 (108): By the attainment of which [vigor], one causes the qualities (*guṇas*) that are unimpeded to increase (*utkarṣati*).
YS 2.39: Through steadfastness in non-possessiveness comes knowledge of the circumstances of one's past lives.

YBh 2.40: Furthermore, regarding lack of association with others: one who observes the true nature of the body, desiring to abandon even his own body, does not perceive bodily purity despite washing it with earth, water, and so forth; how then could he associate with the bodies of others, which are utterly impure?
Furthermore:
*Yogasūtra* 2.41 (109): "Purity of the *sattva*, cheerfulness, one-pointedness, mastery over the senses, and fitness for the vision of the Self [arise].
The words "[arise]" (*bhavanti*) are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. *Yogabhāṣya* 2.41 (109): [The result] is that these qualities come into being.

YS 2.42: From contentment comes the attainment of unsurpassed happiness; these [other pleasures] are not worth even a sixteenth part of the happiness that comes from the destruction of craving. YS 2.43: Perfection of the body and the senses results from austerity through the destruction of impurity.
YS 2.44: Through self-study, there is communion with the chosen deity. YS 2.45: Perfection in samādhi results from devotion to the Lord (īśvarapraṇidhāna).
YBh 2.45: Consequently, his wisdom perceives things as they truly are.

The restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), along with their supernatural attainments (*siddhi*), have been described. We shall now explain the postures (*āsana*) and the others. Among them: *Yoga Sūtra* 2.46: "A posture is firm and pleasant.

*Yoga Bhāṣya* 2.46: For example, the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), the auspicious posture (*bhadrāsana*), the cross-legged posture (*svastika*), the staff posture (*daṇḍāsana*), the supported posture (*sapāśraya*), the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), the crane-sitting posture (*krauñcaniṣadana*), the elephant-sitting posture (*hastiniṣadana*), the camel-sitting posture (*uṣṭraniṣadana*), the balanced stance (*samasaṃsthāna*), and whatever is firm and pleasant, as well as whatever is comfortable—these and others are [postures].
YS 2.47: [Posture is mastered] through the relaxation of effort and through meditative absorption on the infinite.
YS 2.48: From that, there is no affliction by the pairs of opposites.
YBh 2.48: By virtue of mastery over posture, one is not overcome by the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat.
YS 2.49: When that [posture] is attained, the interruption of the flow of inhalation and exhalation is breath control (prāṇāyāma).
The interruption of their flow is the cessation of both; this is breath control.
YBh 2.50: But that—
The third [type of breath control] has the nature of suppression (*stambha*), wherein there is the simultaneous absence of both [inhalation and exhalation] through a single effort.

Observed by means of numbers: with so many inhalations and exhalations, there is the first *udghāta* (upward surge); likewise, for one who has restrained [the breath], with so many [breaths] there is the second *udghāta*, and similarly the third.
Thus, it is observed by numbers as being mild, moderate, or intense.

YBh 2.51 (113): [The breath] is drawn out by external objects through [specification of] place, time, and number; likewise, it is drawn out by internal objects. In both cases, it becomes long and subtle.

YS 2.52: From that, the veil over the light [of knowledge] is destroyed. YBh 2.52: For this yogi who practices breath control (prāṇāyāma), the karma that veils discriminative knowledge is destroyed—that which they call [the "impurity"]. YBh 2.52: [They describe it as follows: "O Maitreya, that which is called impurity is a subtle substance consisting of the quality of darkness (tamas); by its conjunction with the intellect (buddhi), it covers the light of knowledge. It is this very thing that is destroyed by the practice of breath control. Furthermore, it is said: "The yogi who practices breath control destroys the impurity that consists of the quality of darkness; therefore, he should practice breath control. Thus, through the destruction of the veil over the light, the mind becomes fit for concentration. Therefore, it has been stated: "From that, the veil over the light is destroyed."
YBh 2.52 (114): Thus, this karma of his—which is the obscuration of light and the bond of saṃsāra—becomes weakened through the practice of prāṇāyāma and is destroyed moment by moment.
And so it has been said:
"There is no austerity higher than prāṇāyāma; from it comes the purification of impurities and the radiance of knowledge."
Furthermore, there is fitness of the mind for the concentrations (dhāraṇās).
This arises precisely from the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), according to the statement: “Or [it is attained] by the expulsion and retention of the vital breath.”
YBh 2.54: Now, what is withdrawal (pratyāhāra)?
YS 2.55: From that comes the supreme mastery over the senses.
YBh 2.55: Some say that victory over the senses consists in not being addicted to sound and the other objects of the senses.
Attachment...is addiction, for it casts one away from the highest good.
Some say that mastery over the senses consists in the cognition of sound and other objects when they are not opposed [to dharma] and are devoid of pleasure and pain.
Jaigīṣavya, however, maintains that it is simply non-apprehension resulting from one-pointedness of mind.
The five external means of practice have been described.
Now, concentration (*dhāraṇā*) must be explained.
Yoga Sūtra 3.1: Concentration is the binding of the mind to a particular location.
YS 3.2: Therein, the one-pointed flow of cognition is *dhyāna* (meditation).
YS 3.3: That same [state], when it manifests as the object alone and is, as it were, devoid of its own nature, is *samādhi* (concentration).
YS 3.4: The three [—*dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi*] combined in one place constitute *saṃyama*.

YBh 3.4 (120): This triad of dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi, when applied to a single object, is saṃyama. These three means directed toward one and the same object are called saṃyama. This technical term for this triad in the system is "saṃyama."
YS 3.5 (120): From mastery over that [dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi], there is the light of wisdom. YS 3.6 (120): Its application is upon the stages [of yoga].
YBh 3.6 (121): For one who has not mastered a lower stage cannot attain mastery (*saṃyama*) on the final stages by skipping over the immediately succeeding stage.
And because of the absence of that [object], how could there be for him the light of wisdom?
Why? Because its object has been understood from another source alone.
How so? For it has been stated thus:
YS 3.7: These three are internal compared to the preceding ones.
YS 3.8: Even these are external to the seedless [samādhi].
YBh 3.8: Even those three internal means are external to seedless yoga. Why?
The mind follows the moment of cessation; this transformation of the conditioning factors (*saṃskāra*) of a single mind at every moment is the transformation of cessation (*nirodha-pariṇāma*).
(YS 3.9) Its flow becomes tranquil through the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
(YS 3.10) The tranquil flow of the mind depends upon proficiency gained through the practice of the latent impressions of cessation. (YBh 3.10)
YBh 3.11 (123): The capacity for all objects is a property of the mind.
One-pointedness is also a property of the mind.
The meaning is that the destruction of the capacity for all objects is its disappearance.
YBh 3.11 (123–124): The meaning is that there is an emergence and absorption into one-pointedness.

Thus, this mind, following after two dharmas that have become its own nature—the disappearance of the former and the appearance of the latter—is concentrated; that is the transformation of the mind into concentration (*samādhi*).
YS 3.12 (124): Thereafter, when the subsided and the arisen cognitions are identical, that is the transformation of the mind into one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*).
YBh 3.12 (124): For one whose mind is concentrated, the preceding cognition is tranquil, while the succeeding one, being similar to it, has arisen;
the mind of concentration follows both, and thus it remains exactly as it was until there is a lapse from concentration.
This, indeed, is the transformation of the mind—the substratum—into one-pointedness.
In this regard, the suppression of emergence and the manifestation of cessation constitute the transformation of attributes (*dharma-pariṇāma*) within the substrate (*dharmin*).
There is also the transformation of temporal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-pariṇāma*); cessation possesses three characteristics and is endowed with the three time-periods (*adhvan*).
Furthermore, it is not dissociated from the past and future characteristics.

Likewise, emergence possesses three characteristics and is connected with the three time-periods; having abandoned the present characteristic while not transcending its essential nature (*dharmatva*), it has entered into the past characteristic.
And yet, it is not devoid of the future and present characteristics.
Similarly, when emergence again occurs, having abandoned the future characteristic while not transcending its essential nature, it has entered into the present characteristic.
Nor is it devoid of the two characteristics of the past and the future.
Thus there is suppression again, and thus there is emergence again.
This is the transformation of state (*avasthā-pariṇāma*) of dharmas.
Thus, through the transformations of dharma, characteristic, and state, the activity of the guṇas does not remain still for even a moment.
And the activity of the guṇas is mobile;
indeed, it has been stated that the inherent nature of the guṇas is the cause of their activity.
YBh 3.13 (126): From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), however, there is only one single transformation (*pariṇāma*).
YBh 3.13 (127): Just as when a golden vessel is broken and fashioned into something else, there is a change of state (*bhāvānyathātva*) but no change in the gold itself.
YBh 3.13 (127): This objection [is invalid] because we do not admit absolute [identity].
YBh 3.13 (128): Even that which has departed exists, because its destruction is denied.
And its subtlety results from its association [with other elements], and from its subtlety there is non-perception.

The rebuttal to that [objection] is as follows: it cannot be established that things possess the nature of being "things" (dharmatva). Furthermore, it has been stated that specific qualities (*rūpa-atiśaya*) and specific functions (*vṛtti-atiśaya*) are mutually exclusive, whereas generalities (*sāmānya*) coexist with those specificities.
Therefore, there is no confusion [of the guṇas], just as when passion is manifest in a particular instance, it does not mean that it is absent elsewhere at that time.

Just as the configuration (saṃsthāna) of the qualities (guṇas) such as sound—which are subject to destruction and non-destruction—is a beginningless attribute alone, so too the subtle body (liṅga) is a beginningless attribute alone of the qualities such as sattva, which are subject to destruction and non-destruction; this is what is designated as "modification" (vikāra).

YBh 3.13 (132): These transformations of dharma, characteristic, and state do not transcend the essential nature of the substratum (*dharmin*); thus, there is only one transformation that encompasses all these particularities.
YBh 3.14 (132): In this regard, YS 3.14 (132):
The substratum conforms to its dharmas, whether they are past (*śānta*), present (*udita*), or yet to be designated (*avyapadeśya*).
YBh 3.14 (132): Dharma is indeed the power (*śakti*) of the substratum (*dharmin*), as delimited by its capacity (*yogyatā*).

In that context, the substratum, while existing and undergoing its own activity, is distinguished from other dharmas—namely, those that have subsided (*śānta*), those yet to arise (*udita*), and those that are indeterminable (*avyapadeśya*).
Regarding this, the dharmas of the substratum are indeed of three kinds: the subsided, the arisen, and the indeterminable.

In that regard, those [dharmas] which have become tranquil and have ceased their activity are the past; those with activity are the present, and they are immediate to the future characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Those that are past are immediate to the present. Why are the present ones not immediate to the past? Because there is no such priority and posteriority for the past. (YBh 3.14, p. 133) Now, what are the "indescribable" (*avyapadeśya*) [dharmas]? Everything has everything as its nature.
YBh 3.14 (133): Regarding this, it has been stated—that the transformational diversity of taste and other qualities in water and earth is observed among stationary objects.
YBh 3.14 (134): Indeed, due to the constraints of place, time, form, and cause, the manifestation of these [qualities] does not occur simultaneously for all selves.
YBh 3.14 (134): For one, however, for whom this [world] is merely dharma (mental impression) without any underlying substrate, there is an absence of experience.
YBh 3.14 (134): And the absence of memory for that [object] is because one person cannot remember what was seen by another.
YBh 3.15 (135): For example, there is a sequence such as powder, clay, a lump of clay, a jar, potsherds, and fragments of clay.
YBh 3.15 (135): "The lump ceases and the jar arises"—this is the sequence of the transformation of attributes (*dharmapariṇāmakrama*). [The roots *pra-cyu* and *upa-jan* are used here.]

YBh 3.15 (135): Why [is there no sequence]? Because "immediacy" exists only when there is a relation of "prior and posterior," yet such a relation does not exist for that which is past; therefore, sequence occurs only between two characteristics.
YBh 3.15 (135): Two types of dharmas are observed in the mind: those that are perceived and those that are unperceived.

YBh 3.15 (135): "In that regard, those consisting of cognition are perceived, while those consisting of the mere substance are unperceived; activity and power are properties of the mind that are beyond [ordinary] perception. YS 3.16 (137): Through *saṃyama* upon the three transformations, there arises knowledge of the past and the future.
YBh 3.16 (137): Through *saṃyama* upon the transformations of characteristics (*dharma*), time-periods (*lakṣaṇa*), and states (*avasthā*), knowledge of the past and future arises for yogins.
YBh 3.16 (137): The triad of *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi* performed upon a single object is called *saṃyama*.
YBh 3.16 (137): By means of that, the threefold transformation being directly perceived brings about knowledge of the past and future regarding those [transformations].

YS 3.17: Due to the mutual superimposition of word, object, and cognition, there is a confusion among them; through *saṃyama* upon their distinction, knowledge of the cries of all beings arises. YBh 3.17 (137–138):

Furthermore, the auditory organ has as its object only the transformation of sound (*dhvani*). YBh 3.17 (138): A word (*pada*), however, is to be grasped by the intellect through the synthesis of successive sounds (*nāda*).

YBh 3.17 (138): Because phonemes cannot exist simultaneously, they are by nature mutually independent; they appear and disappear without having touched or established a word. Thus, each individual phoneme is said to lack the nature of a word. YBh 3.17 (142): He who knows their distinction is all-knowing.
Likewise, there is no action without a means.

"...lives... means he sustains the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). YBh 3.17 (143): There is a distinction among those—word, object, and cognition. YBh 3.17 (143–144): For example, in the expression "the palace is white," the word has action as its meaning.
The word "white palace" has the sense of a *kāraka* (a factor of action); its referent (*artha*) consists of both the action and the factors of action, and so does the cognition (*pratyaya*).
Why? Because this convention (*saṃketa*) is a cognition of a single form, arising from the connection [of the parts] as "this is that. (YBh 4.17)
YBh 3.17 (144): Thus, through *saṃyama* on the differentiation of that [speech], the yogin’s knowledge of the cries of all living beings is accomplished.
YS 3.18 (144): From the direct perception of *saṃskāras*, knowledge of previous births arises.

YBh 3.18 (144): Those *saṃskāras* are mental qualities (*cittadharma*) formed by the impressions of previous existences; like transformation, activity, cessation, power, and the quality of life-force (*jīvana*), they are imperceptible.
Mastery over these [past and future lives] is capable of bringing about the direct perception of *saṃskāras*.
And there can be no direct perception of them without [knowledge of] their place, time, causes, and experiences.
Thus, from the direct perception of *saṃskāras*, knowledge of previous births arises for the yogin.
YBh 3.18 (145): Likewise, by directly perceiving the *saṃskāras* in others as well, there arises knowledge of their births.
Regarding this, the following narrative is heard:
"Is even this supreme mastery over primordial matter (*pradhāna*) belonging to the Venerable One, and this unsurpassed happiness of contentment, to be categorized on the side of suffering?"
YBh 3.18 (145): But because of the departure from the torment of thirst and suffering, this [state] is said to be happiness that is serene, unafflicted, and favorable in every respect.
YS 3.19 (146): From the cognition [of another's mental state], there is knowledge of the mind of another.
YS 3.20 (146): And that [knowledge] does not have an objective support, because that [other's mind] has not become an object for it.
By this, the disappearance of sound and the other objects [of the senses] should be understood as explained.

(YS 3.22) Karma is either with onset (*sa-upakrama*) or without onset (*nirupakrama*); through *saṃyama* upon that, there arises knowledge of the end of life, or from portents (*ariṣṭa*). (YBh 3.22) Karma that ripens as lifespan is of two kinds: with onset and without onset.
And just as that very same [mass of water], when condensed, would dry up in a long time, so too is [the life] without exertion (*nirupakrama*).
At that time, the karma that produces the lifespan for a single birth is of two kinds: with exertion (*sa-upakrama*) and without exertion (*nirupakrama*).
Through mastery (*samyama*) over that, there arises knowledge of the end, namely, the time of death (*prāyaṇa*).
YBh 3.22 (147): "Or from portents," etc.; portents are threefold: internal (*ādhyātmika*), elemental (*ādhibhautika*), and celestial (*ādhidaivika*).
[Internal, elemental, celestial.
YBh 3.22 (147): Likewise, the elemental portent consists in seeing the messengers of Yama.
One suddenly sees deceased ancestors;
likewise, one suddenly sees the celestial realm or perfected beings (siddhas) belonging to the divine sphere;
or else, everything appears in a contrary manner. By this, one knows that the end of life is at hand.
YS 3.23: [The yogic] powers arise from [the practice of] friendliness and so forth.
YBh 3.23: That concentration which arises from cultivation is *saṃyama*; from that, powers are born whose vigor is no longer barren.
Furthermore, because there is no concentration regarding that [equanimity], there is no power arising from equanimity, due to the absence of *saṃyama* therein.
YS 3.25: By directing the light of the mind toward the *pravṛtti* (the course of evolution), there arises knowledge of the subtle, the concealed, and the distant.
YBh 3.26: Its expansion consists of the seven worlds (*loka*).
Thus is the summary verse (saṃgrahaśloka).
Therein, living beings who experience the suffering acquired through their own karma are born after having drawn out a miserable and long lifespan.
Thence follow the seven netherworlds (pātāla) known as Mahātala, Rasātala, Talātala, Sutala, Vitala, Talātala, and Pātāla.
This is the eighth stage: the earth consisting of seven continents.
Its peaks are composed of silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, gold, and jewels;
the eastern peak is white.
The western [side] is clear,
and the northern has the luster of kuraṇṭaka flowers.
Due to the movement of the sun, night and day proceed as if attached to it.

YBh 3.26 (146): To its north are three mountains—Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgavat—each two thousand [yojanas] in extent. YBh 3.26 (146): To the south are Niṣadha, Hemakūṭa, and Himavat, each two thousand [yojanas] in extent.
YBh 3.26 (147): Beyond these, the islands of Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śālmala, Gomeda (and Plakṣa) are each double the size of the preceding one.

The Puṣkara continents and the oceans are like heaps of mustard seeds, adorned with various mountain peaks, and filled with the juices of sugarcane, wine, clarified butter, whey, milk, and sweet water.
Sumeru is the pleasure garden of the Thirty-three gods; therein are the gardens known as Miśravana, Nandana, Caitraratha, and Sumānasa.
YBh 3.26 (147): [There are] the Sudharmā assembly hall of the gods, the city of Sudarśana, and the Vaijayanta palace.
YBh 3.26 (148): There are six classes of gods residing in the realm of Mahendra: the Tridaśas, the Agniṣvāttas, the Yāmyas, the Tuṣitas, the Aparinirmitavaśavartins, and the Parinirmitavaśavartins.
YBh 3.26 (152): Among them, the Acyutas experience the bliss of dhyāna accompanied by vitarka.
The Śuddhanivāsa [deities] possess the bliss of dhyāna accompanied by vicāra;
the Satyābhā [deities] possess the bliss of dhyāna consisting of pure ānanda;
and the Saṃjñāsaṃjñin [deities] possess the bliss of dhyāna consisting of pure asmitā.
YBh 3.26 (152): All these seven worlds are indeed the Brahma-worlds.
One should practice in this manner even elsewhere until all of this has been seen. YBh 3.31 (153):
Below the navel, within the chest, there is a channel shaped like a tortoise.
Or, through intuitive insight (*prātibha*), everything [is known].
From that, intuitive insight, hearing, touch, sight, taste, and awareness arise.
Through intuitive insight, there is knowledge of the subtle, the concealed, the distant, the past, and the future.
YBh 3.36 (156): From hearing [sounds], there is the perception of divine sounds; from feeling [touch], there is the attainment of divine touch;

from seeing [forms], there is the cognition of divine forms; from tasting, there is the cognition of divine tastes; and from smelling, there is the discernment of divine fragrances—these arise constantly. YS 3.38 (156): Through the loosening of the cause of bondage and through the awareness of the movement of the mind, entry into another’s body occurs.

YBh 3.38: And when the mind is withdrawn [into itself], the senses follow after it. YS 3.39: Through mastery over the *uddāna* [vital breath], there is non-attachment to water, mud, thorns, and so forth, as well as the power of exiting [the body].
YBh 3.39: The function of all the senses, characterized by the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so on, is life.
Its function is fivefold: *prāṇa* is the movement through the mouth and nose, its operation extending as far as the heart;
*samāna* is so called because it leads [the nutrients] equally, and its operation extends as far as the navel.

Of these, *prāṇa* is the primary one. Through mastery over *udāna*, there arises non-attachment to water, mud, thorns, and the like, as well as the power of departure (*utkrānti*) at the time of death; he attains mastery over that.
YS 3.40: From mastery over the *samāna* [vital air], there is the kindling of light.
YBh 3.40: Having mastered the *samāna*, one performs the fanning of the vital energy (*tejas*) and thereby kindles it.
YS 3.41: Through *saṃyama* on the connection between the auditory organ and space, there is divine hearing.

YBh 3.41 (158–159): Space is the support of all auditory organs and of all sounds. As it has been stated—that for all [beings] whose hearing occurs in the same location, there is a single locus of audition for all—this is a mark (*liṅga*) of space. Furthermore, non-obstruction has been stated; and since that which is formless is seen to be unobstructed, the all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) of space is also well-known. The auditory organ is inferred from the perception of sound. [Inference]

YS 3.43: The external function [of the mind] that is not imagined is the "Great Bodiless" (mahāvideha); from that comes the destruction of the veil over light. YBh 3.43: But that which is independent of the body—the external function of the mind itself when it has become external—is indeed the "unimagined" (akalpita). In this regard, they accomplish the unimagined Great Bodiless by means of the imagined [bodiless state]. YBh 3.43: By means of this, yogins enter into the bodies of others.
YS 3.44: Through *saṃyama* upon the gross form, the subtle nature, the inherence, and the purposiveness [of the elements], mastery over the elements (*bhūtajaya*) is attained.

YBh 3.44 (162): Of this generality, sound and the other [qualities] are the particulars. And so it has been said: "For these things which are endowed with a single genus, there is the exclusion of their mere attributes.

YBh 3.44 (163): And that [generality] is intended to be expressed in terms of both difference and non-difference, as in the expressions "a forest of mango trees" (*āmraṇāṃ vanam*) or "an assembly of Brahmins" (*brāhmaṇānāṃ saṃghaḥ*), where one says "a mango-forest" (*āmra-vanam*) or "a Brahmin-assembly" (*brāhmaṇa-saṃghaḥ*).
Now, what is their subtle form?
It is the *tanmātra*, the cause of the gross elements.
Furthermore, their fifth form is *arthavattva* (the state of possessing a purpose).
YS 3.45: From that [mastery of the mind], there arises the manifestation of the powers such as *aṇimā*, the perfection of the body, and non-obstruction by its qualities.
YBh 3.45: Among these, *aṇimā* is becoming minute; *laghimā* is becoming light; *mahimā* is becoming large;
and it means entering even through a stone.
YS 3.46: Perfection of the body consists in beauty, grace, strength, and adamantine solidity.

YS 3.47: Mastery over the senses results from *saṃyama* (mastery) with respect to their [fivefold] nature: their capacity for grasping, their essential form, their egoistic nature (*asmitā*), their commonality, and their purposefulness.

YBh 3.47: The senses are the particulars of that [commonality]. The fourth form is the guṇas—characterized by illumination, activity, and inertia—which, together with the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), undergo transformation into the senses as their determinative essence.

YBh 3.47: When the yogin has achieved mastery over each of these five forms of the senses through sequential *saṃyama*, mastery over the senses arises from that mastery over their five forms. YS 3.48: From that, there arise swiftness of mind, the state of being without organs (*vikaraṇabhāva*), and mastery over primordial matter (*pradhāna*). YS 3.49: For one who possesses only the discriminative discernment of the difference between the *sattva* and the Puruṣa, there arises sovereignty over all states of being and omniscience.

YBh 3.50 (168): Thus, for one who becomes dispassionate toward that [mind], those seeds of affliction—which are like burnt rice seeds and incapable of germination—perish along with the mind itself. YS 3.52 (170): From *saṃyama* on the moment and its sequence, knowledge born of discrimination arises. YBh 3.52 (171): Indeed, all these attributes (*dharma*) are mounted upon the moment. Through *saṃyama* on that moment and its sequence, there is direct perception of them; and from that, knowledge born of discrimination manifests.
YBh 3.53 (171): A specific distinction regarding its object is now proposed.

YBh 3.53 (173): However, the differentiation of moments is accessible only to the intellect of a yogin; therefore, Vārṣagaṇya has said that because there is no difference in form, spatial separation, or genus, there is no fundamental distinctness [between atoms].
YS 3.54 (174): The knowledge born of discrimination is "star-like" (tāraka), having all things as its object, having all aspects as its object, and being non-sequential.

YBh_3.54(174): "Star-like" (*tāraka*) means that it arises from one's own intuition and is not derived from instruction. "Having all things as its object" means that there is nothing whatsoever that does not become an object for it.
YBh_3.54(174): "Having everything as its object in every way" means that it knows everything—past, future, and present—in all its modes and in every respect.
YBh_3.55(174): [This applies] to one who has attained the knowledge born of discrimination, or to one who has not yet attained it.

YBh 3.55 (175): When the *sattva* of the intellect (*buddhisattva*), its stains of *rajas* and *tamas* having been shaken off, has fulfilled its sole purpose—which is the discernment of the distinctness of the *puruṣa*—and the seeds of affliction have been burnt away, then it attains, as it were, a state of similarity with the *puruṣa*. At that time, the absence of the *puruṣa*'s imputed experience is purity. In this state, there is isolation (*kaivalya*) for one who possesses knowledge born of discrimination, whether they be a Lord (*īśvara*) or not, or anyone else.
YBh 3.55 (175): For that person, there is isolation (kaivalya). YBh 4.1 (176): Through austerity (tapas), there is the perfection of will (saṃkalpasiddhi).
YBh 4.2 (177): In that regard, [there is the transformation] of the body and senses, which have undergone a change of species.
YS 4.2: Transformation into another species occurs through the influx of *prakṛti*. YBh 4.2:

The disappearance of a prior transformation and the emergence of a subsequent transformation occur due to the entry of new constituent parts (*avayava*). YS 4.3: An external cause is not the motivator of the *prakṛtis*; rather, it serves to break the obstruction, like a farmer [who irrigates a field].
But the breaking of the obstruction occurs from that [practice], like a farmer.
YBh 4.3 (178): Or, for example, that very same farmer is not able to cause watery or earthy juices to enter the roots of the grain in that very field;
rather, he removes the mudga beans, gavedhukā grass, śyāmāka millet, and so forth from it.
When those [impurities] have been removed, the juices themselves enter into the roots of the grain,
because purity and impurity are absolutely contradictory;
(YS 4.4) the created minds arise from the mere state of "I-am-ness" (asmitā).

YBh 4.4 (178): Taking as its material cause the mere state of "I-am-ness" (asmitāmātra), which is the cause of the mind, it creates minds of transformation; therefore, they become possessed of mind. YS 4.5 (179): In the case of a diversity of activities, there is a single directing mind for many [minds].
YBh 4.5 (179): How is it that the activity of many minds proceeds preceded by the intention of a single mind? [The answer is: It creates one presiding mind for all the minds;
from that, the differentiation of activity arises.
YS 4.6 (179): Among these, that which is born of meditation is free from latent impressions (*anāśaya*).
YBh 4.7 (180): Since... YS 4.7 (180): For the yogi, karma is neither-white-nor-black; for others, it is of three kinds.
YBh 4.7 (180): This class of karma indeed consists of four categories: black, white-and-black, white, and neither-white-nor-black.
Among these, the black [karman] belongs to the evil-minded; the white-and-black belongs to those who accomplish their goals through external means.
Among these, the accumulation of the storehouse of karman occurs solely by way of harming or favoring others; the white [karman] belongs to those devoted to austerity, self-study, and meditation.

YBh 4.7 (180): [Karma] is neither white nor black for renunciants whose afflictions have been exhausted and who possess only their skin-encased bodies. Among these, it is "not white" because the yogi has renounced the fruits [of action], and it is "not black" because of the absence of appropriation. For other beings, however, all three types [of karma] exist as before. YS 4.8 (180): From that, there is the manifestation only of those latent dispositions (*vāsanā*) which are conducive to the ripening of that [karma].
YBh 4.8 (181): "From that" means from the threefold karma.

"Only those [impressions] that are conducive to that maturation" means: whatever kind of karma there is, its maturation is such that the impressions which are conducive to it—those which lie latent following the maturation of the karma—are alone manifested.
(YS 4.9) Even for those [impressions] separated by birth, place, and time, there is immediate succession because memory and the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) are of a single nature.
(YBh 4.9) The arising of the maturation of a cat is manifested by its own manifesting cause.

YBh 4.9 (181): Why? Because even for these [impressions] that are separated by time and space, there exists a similar action (*karman*) which, having become the cause (*nimitta*), manifests them; thus, there is indeed immediate succession (*ānantarya*). And why [is this so]? Because memory (*smṛti*) and latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) are of one and the same nature. As were the experiences, so are the impressions. And those [impressions] conform to the latent tendencies of karma (*karmavāsanā*). As are the latent tendencies, so is the memory. Thus, from latent impressions separated by birth, place, and time, memory arises.

YS 4.10: And their beginninglessness is due to the eternity of the desire for self-preservation. YBh 4.10: These latent impressions (vāsanās) are beginningless because the desire for self-preservation is eternal. This desire for self-preservation—“May I not cease to be; may I continue to exist”—is observed in everyone, and it is not inherent by nature. YBh 4.11: Therefore, this mind, permeated by beginningless latent impressions, manifests for the experience of the Puruṣa by seizing upon certain specific impressions through the influence of external causes.

YBh 4.10 (183): Others maintain that the mind, like a lamp placed in a jar or a palace, undergoes contraction and expansion and is merely the size and shape of the body; in this way, both the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) are logically accounted for. YBh 4.10 (184): The Teacher [Vyāsa] maintains that it is simply the activity (*vṛtti*) of the all-pervading (*vibhu*) mind that undergoes contraction and expansion. And that [activity] depends upon causes such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth. Furthermore, the cause is of two kinds: external and internal.
External [dharma] depends on means such as the body, including praise, giving, and salutation; internal [dharma], such as faith and so forth, is dependent upon the mind alone.
Of these two, the mental is more powerful.
But as for the fruit: that which, depending upon this [present object], brings about the manifestation of dharmas and so forth, does not involve the production of something previously non-existent.
Whatever object has become manifest reveals a certain latent impression (*vāsanā*); that object is the objective support (*ālambana*) of that impression.

YBh 4.11 (185): Thus, all latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are comprised by these [categories of] cause, fruit, substratum, and object. In the absence of these, there is also the absence of the latent impressions which depend upon them.

YBh 4.12 (186): Since that which is non-existent cannot come into being, and that which is existent cannot perish, how can latent impressions—which exist as substantial entities—be brought to cessation?
YS 4.12: The past and the future exist in their own nature through the differentiation of the temporal paths (*adhvan*) of the *dharmas*.
YBh 4.12: That whose manifestation is yet to come is the future; that whose manifestation has been experienced is the past; and that which is engaged in its own activity is the present.
All three of these are real entities (*vastu*) and are objects of knowledge for cognition.

YBh 4.12 (186): "And if this [past and future] did not exist by way of its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), then this cognition devoid of an object would not have arisen. Therefore, the past and the future exist by way of their own nature;
whereas that which has come within the range of vision is utterly insubstantial, like an illusion."
YBh 4.14 (188): But when all [the guṇas] are [present], how can there be a single sound or a single sense organ?
YS 4.14 (188): The reality of things [is established] because of the unity of their transformation.
YBh 4.15 (190): And for what reason is it improper [to deny this]?

YBh_4.15(191): A single object that serves as a common support for many mental factors (*caitta*) is indeed not imagined by a single mind, nor is it imagined by multiple minds; rather, it is self-established.
Furthermore, it becomes the cause for a cognition arising in conformity with its specific characteristics (*nimitta*), appearing in this or that particular form.

YBh 4.15 (191): Some say... YS 4.16 (192): Nor is an object dependent on a single mind; for if that [mind] were absent, what would become of it? YS 4.17 (193): Because the mind depends upon its coloring by that [object], the object is known or unknown.
YBh 4.17 (193): Objects, which are like magnets, color the mind—which possesses properties similar to iron—by coming into contact with it.
But for one to whom that very mind is the object, [the situation is different].
There might be a doubt that the mind itself will appear as both its own form and the form of the object, like fire—[but] YS 4.19: It does not appear by itself, because it is an object of perception.
Just as the other sense organs and the objects such as sound do not appear by themselves because they are objects of perception, so too the mind is to be understood.
YS 4.20: Furthermore, there is no determination of both [action and agent] at a single moment.
For the proponent of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*), the admission is that existence itself is the action and that very same thing is the agent. YBh 4.21:
And there would be a confusion of memory.
There would be as many memories as there are experiences of cognitions by cognitions.
And due to the confusion of these, there would be an inability to determine a single memory. Thus, by the nihilists who deny the Puruṣa—the witness of the intellect—all has been thrown into disorder.
How so?
And so it has been said:
"Therefore, this is accepted:
the mind, colored by the seer and the seen, has all things as its object. (YS 4.23)

This very mind, colored by the seer and the seen, appearing as both object and subject, assuming the nature of both the conscious and the unconscious, though its essence is the object, yet as if it were not the object, though unconscious, yet as if conscious—resembling a crystal gem, it is said to be "all-pervading" (sarvārtha).
Why are those [objects] not to be inferred? Because there exists the seed of error: that the mind appears in the form of all things.

YBh 4.23 (199): Thus, by distinguishing the mind according to the different natures of the grasper, the grasping, and the grasped, those who possess right vision classify these three according to their respective types; it is by them that the Puruṣa is realized.
YBh 4.24 (199): And for what reason? YS 4.24 (199):
Although variegated by its innumerable latent impressions (*vāsanās*), [the mind] exists for the sake of another, because it functions as a composite whole.
It does not act for its own sake because it lacks the capacity for collective action, like a house;

the mind of happiness is not for the sake of happiness, nor is knowledge for the sake of knowledge—both of these are for the sake of another. For one who perceives the distinction [between Puruṣa and Prakṛti], there is the cessation of the cultivation of self-identification. (YS 4.25)
But that [identification] ceases for one who perceives the distinction. Why? Because this manifold transformation belongs to the mind alone;
however, when ignorance is absent, the Puruṣa is pure and untouched by the attributes of the mind.
Consequently, the cultivation of self-existence ceases for the one who is skilled.

YS 4.26: Then the mind becomes inclined toward discernment and tends toward isolation (*kaivalya*). YBh 4.26: At that time, that mind of his which previously tended toward objects and was inclined toward ignorance undergoes a transformation; it now tends toward isolation and is inclined toward knowledge born of discernment. YS 4.28: Their abandonment has been explained in the same manner as that of the afflictions (*kleśa*).

However, the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of knowledge are not considered here, because they persist until the completion of the mind's task. (YS 4.30) From that [attainment], there is the cessation of afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma.

(YBh 4.30) Through the acquisition of that [knowledge], the afflictions such as ignorance (*avidyā*) are eradicated along with their roots; and the accumulations of karma (*karmāśaya*), whether wholesome or unwholesome, are destroyed along with their very foundations.

YS 4.31: Then, because knowledge is infinite for one whose impurities of all veils have been removed, the knowable becomes small. YBh 4.31: For one who is liberated from all veils of afflictions and karma, there is infinity of knowledge. In that regard, when it has become free from all impurities of the veils, then its infinity occurs.
Regarding this, it has been said:

"From that [state], there is the completion of the sequence of transformation of the guṇas, for they have accomplished their purpose" (YS 4.32). Upon the arising of that Cloud of Virtue (dharmamegha), the sequence of transformation of the guṇas—which have accomplished their purpose—comes to an end. For once enjoyment and liberation have been achieved and their sequence completed, they are not able to persist even for a single moment.
YBh 4.33 (204): Furthermore, this eternity is twofold: unchanging (immutable) eternity and transformative eternity.
Among these, unchanging eternity belongs to the *puruṣa*, while transformative eternity belongs to the *guṇas*.
YS 4.34 (207): Isolation (*kaivalya*) is the withdrawal of the *guṇas*—which are now devoid of purpose for the *puruṣa*—or it is the power of consciousness established in its own nature.

YBh 4.34 (207): Kaivalya is the re-absorption (*pratiprasava*) of the *guṇas*, which consist of cause and effect, once they have fulfilled the purposes of the *puruṣa* and become void of those purposes.

It is the state of abiding in one's own nature (*svarūpapratiṣṭhā*), because of the *puruṣa*'s lack of further connection with the *buddhi-sattva*. The power of consciousness (*citiśakti*) alone remains for the *puruṣa*;
its perpetual abiding in that very state is kaivalya.
